Send the last id you handled as Last-Event-ID (or ?since= ; the header wins). The server keeps the last 512 events of each file in memory and answers the ones after your id. When your id is gone (evicted, the server restarted, or another node that was not listening), you get one resync event, whose id is the newest the server has: re-read the file, then carry on from there. In a cluster, the node that runs the file's live room publishes each event to the others, so a stream on any node gets them.

Mint a new token and reconnect. 4003 the same The host revoked the user ( role: none ). Nothing is sent after the revoke. Stop.

At most 100 streams per file on one server: 429 TOO_MANY_STREAMS . Share one stream between your workers. Read and change OpenCanvas canvases from programs: bots, integrations and back-office jobs. Changes land in the live canvas as one transaction, show up for everyone editing it, and are saved to your application like any other edit.

Every operation is under /api/v1 on your OpenCanvas server. The examples on these pages use https://canvas.example.com ; use your own server's public address. https://canvas.example.com/api/v1/files/{fileId} fileId is your file id, the one you use in launch tokens and callbacks. OpenCanvas keeps no files of its own: your application owns users, permissions and files, and OpenCanvas loads and saves through your callbacks ( integration guide ).

The API is off until you turn it on for your host, in its entry of the hosts file: [[host]] id = "acme" api_key = "env:ACME_OC_API_KEY" # the host key, for server-to-server calls [host.flags] api_v1 = true # the default from 0.2.0 (it was off in 0.1.2); false turns it off With api_v1 = false , every /api/v1 call for that host answers 404 with the code API_OFF . User tokens also need a public base URL ( OC_PUBLIC_URL , or [host.api] audience ); see authentication .

The path carries the major version. Within v1 changes are additive : new operations, new optional parameters, new fields in answers. Ignore fields you do not know. A write runs in the file's live room as one transaction : everyone editing the canvas sees it at once, and it is saved to your application by the same autosave as a person's edit ( POST .../commit saves now). If nobody has the file open, OpenCanvas loads it from you, applies the change and saves it straight away. Changes to existing blocks land directly, unless the call sends "mode": "suggest" or the host sets [host.api] default_mode = "suggest" : then they become suggestions that a person accepts in the editor. A batch that deletes more than 5 blocks needs "confirm": true .

h: 5.2.1 Write path: batches, outbound tick, hot WAL in Redis (ADR-028)
t: A room applies updates as they arrive and queues them. At most every 40 ms (armed by the first queued item) it appends the queue as one batch, then sends one merged update frame and one presence frame shared by every peer. Nothing is fanned out before the batch is durable; a failed append closes the room with 1012 and fans nothing out. Without Redis the WAL is room_updates in the database (one guarded multi-row insert per batch; on SQLite one writer task commits many rooms' batches per transaction). A block is a small web component that lives inside a canvas: an OKR tracker, a ticket card, a chart from your own service. You write it once; OpenCanvas runs it in a sandbox, keeps its data in the document, collaborates on it in real time and exports it. Nothing about your block runs on the server.

t: They sign in to your application, not to OpenCanvas. Your backend checks access and signs a short-lived launch token naming the file, the user and the role: view, comment or edit. OpenCanvas trusts that decision for the life of the token, enforces it on every edit, and switches a role live when your app calls the role API. See the integration guide .

p: OpenCanvas FAQ: status, licence, data, sign-in and AI
t: No. Every change saves to your application on a short timer, when the canvas goes idle, when the last person leaves and when the server shuts down. Each save goes through a durable outbox, so a restart resends it. If your copy of the file changed elsewhere, the policy you chose runs: save a copy, or reload.

p: OpenCanvas FAQ: status, licence, data, sign-in and AI
h: We already use Collabora through WOPI. Can we reuse that?
t: Yes. OpenCanvas is a WOPI client: it uses discovery, CheckFileInfo, GetFile, PutFile and PUT_RELATIVE, calls only the WOPISrc URLs on its allow-list, and signs every call to your WOPI host with the WOPI proof headers. Nextcloud's integration works this way. See WOPI mode and Nextcloud .

p: OpenCanvas FAQ: status, licence, data, sign-in and AI
h: How is OpenCanvas different from Collabora Online?
t: They share an integration model and edit different things. Collabora Online edits office documents: text, spreadsheets and presentations. OpenCanvas edits a canvas: blocks, databases and whiteboards in one document. In both, the host application keeps the file and the permissions, and the editor runs the live session and saves back to the host. The project's research note studies Collabora's integration in detail.

p: OpenCanvas FAQ: status, licence, data, sign-in and AI
h: How does it compare with Slack Canvas, Zoom Canvas and Microsoft Loop?
t: Those canvases live inside their vendor's product and the vendor stores the file: Slack, Zoom, or OneDrive and SharePoint for Loop. OpenCanvas is built to be embedded in your own application, stores the file in your application through callbacks, and runs on your own servers. Loop's portable live components have no OpenCanvas equivalent yet; they are planned. The comparison table on the home page has the details, from the vendors' public documentation.

p: OpenCanvas FAQ: status, licence, data, sign-in and AI
h: Which apps does it integrate with?
t: There are ready integrations for Jitsi Meet (a temporary canvas in every meeting), Nextcloud (.ocanvas files through WOPI), Mattermost (canvases in channels) and Element / Matrix (a room widget). Any other web application can embed OpenCanvas with a launch token signed by its backend, or open it as a WOPI client. See Jitsi Meet , Nextcloud , Mattermost , Element / Matrix and the integration guide .

p: OpenCanvas FAQ: status, licence, data, sign-in and AI
h: What can it import and export?
t: It exports Markdown, HTML, JSON, its native .ocanvas file and Word, and PDF when the operator runs the optional Gotenberg sidecar; otherwise the editor prints to PDF. Whiteboards export as SVG and PNG. It imports Markdown, HTML and CSV into a canvas, when the host turns import on: it is off by default. See Operations .

p: OpenCanvas FAQ: status, licence, data, sign-in and AI
h: How many users can one server handle?
t: The project's sizing guide gives up to 1,000 concurrent users on 1 vCPU and 512 MB, and up to 5,000 on 2 vCPU and 2 GB; beyond 5,000, run cluster mode. These figures come from load tests on one laptop, with most people watching and some typing, so measure on your own hardware. Source: docs/22, “In short: up to 1,000 concurrent users on 1 vCPU and 512 MB; up to 5,000 on 2 vCPU and 2 GB; beyond 5,000, cluster mode.” See Capacity and sizing , which also has the nonstop-typing, crash and cluster runs.

p: OpenCanvas FAQ: status, licence, data, sign-in and AI
t: One node runs on SQLite with no database to set up. For more users, run several nodes against MySQL or MariaDB with Redis: each room has one owner node, the other nodes relay to it, and if the owner dies another node takes the room over from its log. See Operations and Architecture .

p: OpenCanvas FAQ: status, licence, data, sign-in and AI
t: The server is written in Rust, on tokio and axum, and ships as one binary or a Docker image. The editor runs in the browser and is built on Tiptap (ProseMirror) with Yjs, the CRDT that merges everyone's edits. Storage is SQLite by default, or MySQL or MariaDB, with Redis for a cluster. See Architecture .

p: OpenCanvas FAQ: status, licence, data, sign-in and AI
h: Does the demo send anything anywhere?
t: No. The demo is the real editor running against a document in your browser, with simulated collaborators. There is no server behind it, and exports that need a server say so. Its assistant plays a scripted run: no model is called and nothing leaves your browser.

p: OpenCanvas FAQ: status, licence, data, sign-in and AI
h: Where does the assistant send my content?
t: Only to the model server the operator configures: the Claude Platform, or a self-hosted model through vLLM, Ollama or llama.cpp. The OpenCanvas server makes that call, never the browser. AI is off unless the operator turns it on for your app. A self-hosted model needs tool calling for the assistant to edit; without it, it can only answer. See AI and MCP . Last changed 2026-11-26 .

What OpenCanvas is for, for whom, what is in scope, and its non-functional targets. Product: OpenCanvas — an embeddable, real-time collaborative canvas (rich document + board) built for integration . Status: draft v0.1, 2026-11-21. Awaiting approval. Owner: schnsrw1@gmail.com

Every product that wants a "Slack/Zoom/Loop-style canvas" today has two bad options: build a collaborative editor from scratch (months of CRDT, cursor, conflict and export work) or adopt a SaaS whose storage, users and permissions are not theirs. Collabora Online solved this for office files: the host keeps files, users and ACLs, the editor does editing. Nobody offers that model for a modern block canvas.

Drop one iframe (or one web component) into any app and its users get a live, multi-cursor canvas — text, tables, images, links, embeds and boards — while the app keeps full ownership of the file, the users and who can do what.

Host owns identity, ACL and storage. OpenCanvas never authenticates users, never decides permissions, never keeps the canonical file. We own editing. Real-time merge, presence, cursors, preview, export, commit back to host. No document persistence beyond a live session. Session state (CRDT snapshot + update tail) is kept only to survive node restarts and to let late joiners catch up; it is deleted after commit + idle TTL. Lightweight. One server binary; SQLite by default; one JS bundle. Runs on a 1 vCPU / 512 MB box for a small team. Scalable. Stateless HTTP, room-affine WebSocket nodes, MySQL

"Built, in review" means the work is merged and verified and waits for the owner's approval. Ideas and requests are welcome as GitHub issues .

OpenCanvas integrates with any third-party application through standardized APIs and SDKs, without depending on specific CasualOffice products. Hosts connect through the documented launch tokens, callbacks, WOPI, REST, postMessage, the <open-canvas> SDK and MCP; nothing in the server or editor assumes a particular host. This keeps the project independent and modular, and open to a broad developer ecosystem (ADR-038).
